hints: Notice the reaction conditions carefully, hot ethanolic NaOH points to one specific type of reaction for halogenoalkanes.
Recall that ethanolic NaOH causes elimination of HBr from bromoethane to leave a two-carbon unsaturated product.
Connect that unsaturated product to the second clue, only one type of compound can decolourise aqueous bromine by addition.
walkthrough:
**Spot the conditions for elimination**

Great start, let's look at what the reagents tell us. Aqueous NaOH gives substitution to an alcohol, but hot ethanolic NaOH gives elimination to an alkene.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{halogenoalkane + hot ethanolic NaOH} \rightarrow \text{alkene + NaBr + H}_2\text{O}$$

**Write the reaction for bromoethane**

Now apply it to our molecule. We remove HBr from $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ and form a C=C double bond.

Chemical equation:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br + NaOH (ethanolic)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{=CH}_2 + \text{NaBr + H}_2\text{O}$$

**Check with the bromine test**

Does this fit the second clue? Yes, perfectly. Ethene is a colourless gas and its double bond undergoes electrophilic addition with bromine, turning orange $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ colourless.

Test equation:
$$\text{CH}_2\text{=CH}_2 + \text{Br}_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{BrCH}_2\text{Br}$$

options.A: 1,2-dibromoethane ($\text{CH}_2\text{BrCH}_2\text{Br}$) is the colourless liquid product formed AFTER ethene reacts with bromine, not the gas formed before. It cannot decolourise bromine further because it is already saturated.
options.B: Ethanol ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$) is formed by nucleophilic substitution when bromoethane is heated with aqueous NaOH, not hot ethanolic NaOH. It is a liquid, not a gas, and it does not decolourise aqueous bromine.
options.C: Ethene ($\text{CH}_2\text{=CH}_2$) is correct. It is formed by dehydrohalogenation (elimination) with hot ethanolic NaOH, it is a colourless gas, and its C=C bond decolourises aqueous bromine by addition to form 1,2-dibromoethane.
options.D: Hydrogen bromide (HBr) is eliminated during the reaction but it immediately reacts with NaOH to form NaBr and water, so it is not collected as the gas. It is also an acidic gas that does not decolourise aqueous bromine.
